title: Hosea 8:1–14
context: Hosea 8:1–14 is the LORD’s word to the northern kingdom, Israel, often called Ephraim, in its last decades before Assyria conquered it (2 Kings 17). The LORD tells the prophet to sound the trumpet, because something like an eagle hovers over the LORD’s house: Israel has broken his covenant and rebelled against his law. The people claim to know him, yet they have rejected what is good. They set up kings without his approval, made idols of silver and gold, and worshiped the calf of Samaria, which a craftsman made and which is no god (compare 1 Kings 12:28–30). They sow the wind and will reap the whirlwind. They have hired lovers among the nations by turning to Assyria, multiplied altars that became places of sin, treated God’s law as strange, and offered sacrifices he does not accept. The chapter says they will return to Egypt (8:13); 11:5 speaks differently about Egypt, and the two are named without forcing a single explanation. Israel has forgotten its Maker, and Judah has trusted in fortified cities. Shared ground: both traditions read the chapter as a call to covenant faithfulness and an honest account of why judgment came, with the political image of hired lovers read soberly as misplaced trust in foreign powers.

verses.text: “Put the trumpet to your lips! Something like an eagle is over the LORD’s house, because they have broken my covenant and rebelled against my law.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the prophet to put the trumpet to his lips, for an eagle is over the LORD’s house because Israel broke his covenant. Arminian readers see an urgent warning sounded before judgment falls, which still gives the people opportunity to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the covenant as the basis for God’s charge against Israel. Both traditions read the eagle as an image of the coming enemy, likely Assyria, and the LORD’s house as the land or people of Israel rather than only a building.

verses.text: They cry to me, ‘My God, we, Israel, acknowledge you!’
verses.arminianNotes: The people cry, "My God, we, Israel, acknowledge you!" Arminians see a claim of relationship that is not matched by obedience, which makes their words hollow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as exposing empty religious profession. Both traditions hold this as shared ground: knowing God is shown by faithfulness, not merely by claiming his name (compare 6:6).

verses.text: Israel has cast off that which is good. The enemy will pursue him.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Israel has cast off what is good, and the enemy will pursue him. Arminian readers see the people’s deliberate rejection of God’s goodness, which leaves them exposed to danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see judgment following the rejection of God’s ways. Both traditions read the good as God himself and his covenant ways, which Israel abandoned.

verses.text: They have set up kings, but not by me. They have made princes, and I didn’t approve. Of their silver and their gold they have made themselves idols, that they may be cut off.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they set up kings and princes without him and made idols of silver and gold to their own ruin. Arminians see political and religious choices made without seeking God, which led to disaster.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see human autonomy in rebellion against God’s rule. Both traditions note the rapid change of kings in Israel’s last years (2 Kings 15), and they hold idolatry and godless politics together as one failure.

verses.text: Let Samaria throw out his calf idol! My anger burns against them! How long will it be until they are capable of purity?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Samaria to throw out its calf, says his anger burns, and asks how long until they are capable of purity. Arminian readers see God’s anger mixed with longing, as he asks how long his people will remain in sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the question as expressing God’s holy displeasure. Both traditions note that the calf worship goes back to Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:28–30), and they read the verse as a call to abandon it.

verses.text: For this is even from Israel! The workman made it, and it is no God; indeed, the calf of Samaria shall be broken in pieces.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the calf came from Israel itself, a craftsman made it, it is no god, and it will be broken to pieces. Arminians see the folly of worshiping what human hands made, which cannot save.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as exposing idolatry as self-made religion. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and compare similar mockery of idols in Isaiah 44:9–20.

verses.text: For they sow the wind, and they will reap the whirlwind. He has no standing grain. The stalk will yield no head. If it does yield, strangers will swallow it up.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they sow the wind and will reap the whirlwind, with grain that yields nothing or is swallowed by strangers. Arminian readers see consequences growing out of choices, magnified in judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s justice in the harvest of sin. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and compare the principle of sowing and reaping in Galatians 6:7.

verses.text: Israel is swallowed up. Now they are among the nations like a worthless thing.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Israel is swallowed up and is now among the nations like a worthless thing. Arminians see the loss of Israel’s distinct calling, as it becomes like any other nation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as describing the result of covenant unfaithfulness. Both traditions read the image as anticipating exile, when Israel would be scattered among the nations.

verses.text: For they have gone up to Assyria, like a wild donkey wandering alone. Ephraim has hired lovers for himself.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they went to Assyria like a lone wild donkey, and Ephraim hired lovers. Arminian readers see misplaced trust in foreign powers, pictured as paying for alliances instead of trusting God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the imagery of hired lovers soberly, as a picture of political alliances that betrayed covenant loyalty. Both traditions compare 2 Kings 15:19–20 and 17:3–4 for Israel’s dealings with Assyria.

verses.text: But although they sold themselves among the nations, I will now gather them; and they begin to waste away because of the oppression of the king of mighty ones.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that though they sold themselves among the nations, he will gather them, and they will waste away under the king of mighty ones. Arminians see God gathering them for judgment rather than rescue, as their alliances bring oppression.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over the results of Israel’s choices. Both traditions read the king of mighty ones as the Assyrian king, though the phrase is not explained further.

verses.text: Because Ephraim has multiplied altars for sinning, they became for him altars for sinning.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Ephraim multiplied altars for sinning, and they became altars for sinning. Arminian readers see worship turned into sin, as altars meant for God became places of false religion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the irony of increasing religious activity that only increased guilt. Both traditions hold this as shared ground: more worship is not better worship if it departs from God’s word.

verses.text: I wrote for him the many things of my law, but they were regarded as a strange thing.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he wrote many things of his law for them, but they treated them as strange. Arminians see God’s clear revelation rejected by a people who regarded it as foreign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as showing that Israel had God’s word in abundance. Both traditions read it as making Israel’s guilt greater, since they had been taught and refused to listen.

verses.text: As for the sacrifices of my offerings, they sacrifice meat and eat it, but the LORD doesn’t accept them. Now he will remember their iniquity, and punish their sins. They will return to Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they sacrifice and eat meat, but he does not accept it; he will punish their sins, and they will return to Egypt. Arminian readers see worship rejected because it was not offered in faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see ritual without obedience as unacceptable. Both traditions read the return to Egypt as a figure for bondage and exile, and they note that 11:5 speaks differently about Egypt, naming the two verses without forcing a single explanation.

verses.text: For Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces; and Judah has multiplied fortified cities; but I will send a fire on his cities, and it will devour its fortresses.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Israel forgot its Maker and built palaces, Judah multiplied fortified cities, and he will send fire on them. Arminians see misplaced trust in human achievement instead of in God who made them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see forgetting God as the root of Israel’s sin. Both traditions note that Judah is included in the warning, and they read the verse as showing that no fortification protects against God’s judgment.
